issues.reason: Align the English subtraction direction with the independently executed numeric residual example.
issues.before: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right. Two axes are compatible when they are equal or one has size one; missing leading axes act like ones. That convenience can silently create a pairwise operation: subtracting predictions [B, 1] from labels [B] produces [B, B], rather than B individual residuals. Explicitly reshape labels, and assert named dimensions at module boundaries. Avoid a plain transpose on higher-dimensional tensors when only the feature and sequence axes should swap.
issues.after: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right. Two axes are compatible when they are equal or one has size one; missing leading axes act like ones. That convenience can silently create a pairwise operation: subtracting labels [B] from predictions [B, 1] (predictions − labels) produces [B, B], rather than B individual residuals. Explicitly reshape labels, and assert named dimensions at module boundaries. Avoid a plain transpose on higher-dimensional tensors when only the feature and sequence axes should swap.

issues.reason: The original direction-preservation wording excluded negative and zero eigenvalues. Clarify the real-vector limitation of the geometric eigenvector explanation. Previous articles use row vectors; stating the SVD convention prevents swapping input and output singular directions.
issues.before: An eigenvector of a square matrix retains its direction under the map, changing only by an eigenvalue. The singular value decomposition works for rectangular matrices too: A = UΣVᵀ. The right singular vectors specify input directions, singular values specify their nonnegative gains, and left singular vectors specify corresponding output directions. Keeping the largest r singular values gives the best rank-r approximation in Frobenius norm, although that matrix error does not directly guarantee task accuracy.
issues.after: An eigenvector of a square matrix is a nonzero vector mapped to a scalar multiple of itself. For real eigenvalues, a negative value reverses its direction and zero maps it to the zero vector. Some real matrices, such as a 90-degree planar rotation, have no real eigenvectors. The singular value decomposition works for rectangular matrices too: A = UΣVᵀ. For the column-vector convention y = Ax, a right singular vector vᵢ is mapped to σᵢuᵢ: V specifies input directions and U output directions. In the row-vector convention y = xW used earlier, W = UΣVᵀ instead maps uᵢᵀ to σᵢvᵢᵀ, so those roles swap. Keeping the largest r singular values gives the best rank-r approximation in Frobenius norm, although that matrix error does not directly guarantee task accuracy.

issues.reason: Separate overfitting under the sampling distribution from distribution shift and evaluation leakage, which require different diagnoses.
issues.before: A model is useful when it performs on examples it did not fit. Overfitting occurs when improvements on training data fail to transfer to the intended deployment distribution. The gap can arise from memorization, excessive model selection, leakage, or genuine distribution shift. More training accuracy is therefore evidence about fitting capacity, not sufficient evidence that a model is ready for a new population.
issues.after: A model is useful when it performs on examples it did not fit. Overfitting means fitting training-specific patterns that fail to generalize to fresh examples from the same data-generating distribution. A deployment failure can also arise from distribution shift, and leakage can make an evaluation misleading; neither is by itself evidence of overfitting. More training accuracy is therefore evidence about fitting capacity, not sufficient evidence that a model is ready for a new population.

issues.reason: Repeated labels alone do not define einsum reduction; omitted output labels and within-operand diagonal selection are distinct rules.
issues.before: Start with a projected tensor shaped [B, T, H·D]. Reshape it to [B, T, H, D], then permute to [B, H, T, D] for attention. The first operation splits a feature axis; the second moves the head axis. Einsum can make a contraction explicit: 'btd,dh->bth' projects features while retaining batch and time. Repeated labels identify contracted dimensions unless they are included in the output labels.
issues.after: Start with a projected tensor shaped [B, T, H·D]. Reshape it to [B, T, H, D], then permute to [B, H, T, D] for attention. The first operation splits a feature axis; the second moves the head axis. Einsum can make a contraction explicit: 'btd,dh->bth' projects features while retaining batch and time. With an explicit output, dimensions whose labels are omitted from that output are summed, whether or not a label repeats across operands. Repeating a label within one operand selects its diagonal; for example, 'ii->i' extracts a diagonal without summing it.

issues.reason: Gradient accumulation equals a combined mean for fixed per-example losses, but batch-dependent operations can change those losses. A CPU BatchNorm counterexample was executed.
issues.before: Divide each by four before backward if the goal is the mean loss over the combined batch. Otherwise the accumulated gradient is four times larger. Unequal microbatch sizes require weighting by valid examples or tokens instead of a simple factor of four.
issues.after: Divide each by four before backward if the goal is the mean loss over the combined batch. Otherwise the accumulated gradient is four times larger. Unequal microbatch sizes require weighting by valid examples or tokens instead of a simple factor of four. Matching a single large-batch gradient also requires the same per-example forward computation: training-mode BatchNorm changes its statistics across microbatches, and stochastic operations need consistent realizations. Loss scaling alone does not guarantee identical updates.

issues.reason: The original statement explicitly assumed zero-mean inputs and was valid under that restriction; the added second-moment derivation clarifies why ReLU requires the factor of two.
issues.before: A preactivation sums fan_in weighted inputs. Under simplifying independence and zero-mean assumptions, its variance scales roughly with fan_in times weight variance times input variance. Xavier initialization balances incoming and outgoing widths, often using variance 2/(fan_in + fan_out). Kaiming initialization accounts for rectification and commonly uses variance 2/fan_in for ReLU forward signal preservation. The chosen mode and activation gain matter; these are not interchangeable names for arbitrary small random weights.
issues.after: A preactivation sums fan_in weighted inputs. Under simplifying independence assumptions and zero-mean weights, preactivation variance scales roughly as fan_in · Var(w) · E[x²]. This becomes fan_in · Var(w) · Var(x) when inputs are also zero-mean. ReLU outputs generally are not: for a symmetric zero-mean preactivation z, E[ReLU(z)²] = Var(z)/2. Xavier initialization balances incoming and outgoing widths, often using variance 2/(fan_in + fan_out). Kaiming initialization accounts for rectification and commonly uses variance 2/fan_in for ReLU forward signal preservation. The chosen mode and activation gain matter; these are not interchangeable names for arbitrary small random weights.

issues.reason: A gradient-norm bound is not a general optimizer-update bound; Adam normalizes gradients and momentum/decay add state-dependent effects.
issues.before: Early training, representation formation, and late refinement may benefit from different update magnitudes. A learning-rate schedule specifies how the optimizer's base step size changes with progress. Warmup gradually increases that rate at the beginning. Gradient clipping instead reacts to the current gradient, preventing an unusually large norm from producing an excessive update. These mechanisms address different situations and should be recorded separately.
issues.after: Early training, representation formation, and late refinement may benefit from different update magnitudes. A learning-rate schedule specifies how the optimizer's base step size changes with progress. Warmup gradually increases that rate at the beginning. Gradient clipping instead reacts to the current gradient and caps its norm. For plain SGD without momentum or decay this bounds the step norm by learning rate times the threshold; adaptive scaling, momentum, or weight decay mean the same bound does not generally apply to the complete parameter update. These mechanisms address different situations and should be recorded separately.

The second query swaps the weights, producing approximately [0.6604, 2.6792]. Notice that the output mixes values, not keys.

claudeBaselineDisposition.reviewerProvenance: Separate parent-run Claude Code output labels its reviewer as Claude (claude-opus-5-5). It was explicitly a reasoning-only pass without tools, browsing or execution. This audit's source checks and execution are by OpenAI Codex.

findings.reason: Accepted: broadcasting claims now cite the official Broadcasting Semantics page; the numerical-computation chapter is not used as their direct support.
Accepted: eigenvectors map to scalar multiples; negative and zero eigenvalues and lack of real eigenvectors are stated explicitly.
Accepted: column and row conventions are explicit; both singular-vector identities were executed on a nonsymmetric matrix.
Accepted as a wording clarification: deterministic Taylor prediction is now called predicted rather than expected.
Accepted: added Algorithm 1 bias corrections and epsilon outside the square root; first-step Adam behavior was executed.
Accepted: an empty RunningMean raises ValueError instead of reporting a misleading zero; final snippet was executed.
Accepted: the exercise now specifies plain git commit and distinguishes documented -a and pathspec behavior. No repository history mutation was needed.
Accepted: explicit-output einsum reduction and within-operand diagonal semantics were corrected and executed.

Accepted as a clarification, not proof that the original restricted claim was false: the original explicitly assumed zero-mean inputs. The general second-moment equation and ReLU symmetry condition now explain the factor of two.

Accepted with a narrower claim: original test-time weight scaling versus inverted training scaling is explained. The suggested whole-network 'equivalent in expectation' phrasing was not adopted; only the masked activation expectation is guaranteed.
Accepted: added the verified SGDR paper and explicitly separated its cosine schedule/restarts from Transformer inverse-square-root decay.
Accepted: output values were recomputed with unrounded float64 softmax weights and checked against SDPA rather than copying the reviewer's rounded hand calculation.
Rejected: this is a nonsequential reference library. A valid prerequisite link to 04-14 is useful; stable IDs and article ordering are preserved.
Accepted: verified Pope et al. arXiv 2211.05102 directly discusses separate prefill/decode configurations and added it to the article.

articleFindings.reason: Changed both the practice explanation and enriched numeric example to explicitly use predictions minus labels/targets. The stored numeric example was independently executed and is correct for this operation.

Added the official Deep Feedforward Networks chapter for computational graphs, chain rule, path summation and backpropagation. Primary-site chapter excerpts directly verify those subjects; Numerical Computation remains for derivative notation and numerical concerns.

Corrected both passages to identify the full batched multi-head attention-weight tensor: 16 matrices use 32 MiB in total, while each 1024 by 1024 FP16 matrix uses 2 MiB. The original total arithmetic was correct.

This is a nonsequential reference library, so a valid prerequisite may have a later ID. The source-reading paragraph already explains that the cache stores keys and values reused by future queries, not old queries; the visible prerequisite links to the dedicated explanation. Stable IDs are preserved.

limitations: No audit guarantees absence of all errors. The full article text was reviewed, but external sources were checked selectively for relevant claims, not exhaustively line by line.

Four large Deep Learning chapters (Machine Learning Basics, Deep Feedforward Networks, Convolutional Networks, and Sequence Modeling) exceeded the web tool's full-page retrieval limit. Relevant primary-site indexed passages were available and inspected; exact implementation claims also used official PyTorch sources. This is a source-access scope limit, not a claim of having read those full pages through the tool.

Rolling Python/PyTorch documentation showed newer online versions than the local Python 3.13.2/PyTorch 2.11.0+cpu test environment. Core claims were checked against the current documentation and relevant CPU behavior; compatibility with every version is not established.

No CUDA execution, AMP GPU training, FlashAttention kernel benchmark, model-scale training, external-dataset experiment or checkpoint-file I/O was performed. In-memory optimizer restoration and mathematical memory/latency calculations do not establish real hardware performance.

Git modes were verified using official documentation without creating commits. OpenReview's verification challenge prevented directly reading that copy of Reddi et al.; the verified primary arXiv copy was used.

Claude's expanded snapshot predates the final 03-11 citation improvement and subsequent accepted corrections/Adam reference addition. The exact deltas and independent verification are documented in expanded-resolutions-01-04.json.
assessment: All 55 assigned articles were fully reviewed and enriched. Thirty consolidated corrections, clarifications or reference improvements across 23 articles are recorded with original and final evidence. Fifty-three actual execution checks passed, including all six stored Python snippets and targeted numerical/API counterexamples. No unresolved substantive scientific defect remains from these reviews; the stated source-access and execution limits still apply.
